title: Specificity calculation by practical examples
learningObjectives: Calculate selector specificity and compare selectors without relying on selector length.

understand.concept: Specificity is the selector weight used by the cascade when competing declarations have reached the specificity comparison. It is commonly written as three columns: ID, class-like selectors, and type selectors.
understand.whyItMatters: It explains why a rule with an ID selector can override a rule with several class selectors, even when the latter appears later.
understand.analogy: Think of a three-column score: IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, and elements/pseudo-elements. Compare the columns from left to right.
understand.analogyLimit: Specificity is not a single total score. One item in a higher column beats any number in a lower column. Cascade origin, importance and layers are considered before specificity.

explain.narrative: Count IDs in the first column (a), classes, attribute selectors and ordinary pseudo-classes in the second (b), and element names and pseudo-elements in the third (c). Compare a, then b, then c. The universal selector and combinators add no specificity. :where() contributes zero; :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument. Inline style attributes are handled separately from this three-column selector count.

examples.code: Specificity sample
examples.explanation: The ID rule has specificity 1-0-0. The later .card .title rule has 0-2-0. The ID rule wins for color because the first column is compared first.
examples.expectedOutput: The element appears according to the winning CSS rule described in the explanation.

practise.guidedTask: Calculate the specificity of .panel p, then compare it with #main p. Predict which color applies before running the page.
practise.independentTask: Write three selectors with different specificity values, record each three-column value, and predict the winning declaration for one shared element.
hints: Do not add the three columns into one ordinary number.
Combinators such as > and spaces do not add specificity.
